prompt: Channel members perform eight key functions. Does each activity help to complete a transaction or to fulfill a completed transaction?

cards.text: A regional distributor shares monthly shopper survey results with a cereal manufacturer.
cards.explanation: Gathering and distributing market intelligence is the information function, which helps complete transactions.

cards.text: A produce cooperative grades apples by size and packs them into two-kilogram family bags.
cards.explanation: Grading, assembling, and packaging shape the offer to buyer needs, which is the matching function.

cards.text: A hardware chain and a power-tool maker agree on wholesale unit prices and delivery dates.
cards.explanation: Reaching an agreement on price and terms so ownership can transfer is the negotiation function.

cards.text: A grocery wholesaler keeps frozen vegetables in temperature-controlled depots and trucks them to stores.
cards.explanation: Transporting and storing goods is physical distribution, which fulfills completed transactions.

cards.text: A building-supply distributor pays the factory upon shipment and gives contractors 60 days to pay.
cards.explanation: Acquiring and using funds to cover the costs of channel work is the financing function.

cards.text: A fashion boutique buys winter coats outright in August and absorbs the loss if a mild winter leaves stock unsold.
cards.explanation: Assuming the financial hazard of holding inventory in the channel is the risk-taking function.

prompt: Count the intermediary levels between the producer and the final buyer. Which channel structure does each case describe?

cases.text: A specialty coffee roaster bags beans at its roastery and ships online orders directly to home subscribers.
cases.explanation: No intermediary sits between the roaster and the consumer, so this is a direct (zero-level) marketing channel.

cases.text: A mattress factory sells its beds to a regional furniture store chain, which sells them to households.
cases.explanation: Only one intermediary level (the retailer) stands between the manufacturer and the consumer.

cases.text: A confectionery maker sells bulk cases to a regional candy wholesaler, which supplies independent corner stores that sell to shoppers.
cases.explanation: Both a wholesaler and a retailer sit between the producer and the final consumer, creating a two-level channel.

cases.text: An orchard sells crates of peaches to families from a stand at the edge of its own farm.
cases.explanation: The grower sells straight to the final buyer with zero intermediary levels.

cases.text: An automaker builds electric sedans at its assembly plant and sells them through authorized retail dealerships to drivers.
cases.explanation: The retail dealer is a single intermediary layer between the manufacturer and the buyer.

prompt: Disagreements over goals, roles, and rewards create channel conflict. Is each dispute an example of horizontal conflict or vertical conflict?

cards.text: Two franchisees of the same pizza chain in adjacent neighborhoods accuse each other of delivering into the other's territory.
cards.explanation: Both pizza shops operate at the same retail level of the channel.

cards.text: A Swiss watchmaker opens a flagship online store that sells directly to collectors at prices lower than its authorized jewelers.
cards.explanation: The conflict is between the manufacturer and its retail jewelers at different levels of the channel.

cards.text: Three farm-equipment dealers in the same province complain that a fourth dealer is advertising below-cost clearance prices.
cards.explanation: All four dealers sit at the same level of the distribution channel.

cards.text: A soft-drink manufacturer and a national supermarket chain clash over promotional allowances and eye-level shelf space.
cards.explanation: A producer and a retailer occupy different levels of the same channel.

cards.text: Two hotel owners operating under the same hotel brand near an airport argue over how loyalty members are routed between them.
cards.explanation: The dispute is between two peers at the same level of the franchise system.

cards.text: An electronics manufacturer raises minimum order quantities, angering the regional wholesalers that stock its cables.
cards.explanation: The disagreement occurs between the producer level and the wholesale level.

prompt: Match each channel organization structure with the business arrangement that exemplifies it.

pairs.match: An independent soap maker, an independent regional distributor, and an independent pharmacy each negotiate every order separately to maximize their own margins.
pairs.explanation: In a conventional channel, separate businesses operate independently with little formal coordination.

pairs.match: An apparel company owns the textile mills, the garment factories, the distribution warehouses, and the retail stores that sell its clothing.
pairs.explanation: A corporate VMS combines successive stages of production and distribution under single ownership.

pairs.match: An automotive service brand licenses its trademark and operating system to 800 independently owned repair shops through binding franchise agreements.
pairs.explanation: A contractual VMS links independent firms at different channel levels through formal contracts such as franchising.

pairs.match: A dominant big-box retailer uses its massive purchasing volume to dictate packaging standards, delivery windows, and shelf replenishment rules to independent suppliers.
pairs.explanation: An administered VMS coordinates successive stages through the size and market power of one dominant member.

prompt: Which channel development does each scenario illustrate: a horizontal marketing system, a multichannel distribution system, or disintermediation?

cases.text: A retail bank and a national supermarket chain partner to place staffed banking booths inside grocery stores.
cases.explanation: Two companies at the same level combine resources to pursue a joint marketing opportunity.

cases.text: A paint manufacturer sells its coatings through its own brand stores, through hardware wholesalers, and through an online contractor portal.
cases.explanation: A single firm sets up two or more marketing channels to reach different customer segments.

cases.text: An airline stops paying commissions to brick-and-mortar travel agencies and sells tickets directly to passengers on its mobile app.
cases.explanation: The service producer cuts out traditional intermediaries to transact directly with final buyers.

cases.text: A local artisan bakery and a specialty tea brand open co-branded airport kiosks to serve travelers together.
cases.explanation: Two peer firms at the same channel level join forces to capture an opportunity neither could easily serve alone.

cases.text: A video-game studio replaces boxed discs sold at electronics stores with direct digital downloads from its own server.
cases.explanation: Replacing physical retail resellers with direct digital delivery is classic disintermediation.

prompt: Match each logistics mechanism with the operational problem it is designed to solve.

pairs.match: Holding harvested grain or seasonal patio furniture for several months until consumer demand peaks.
pairs.explanation: Storage warehouses hold goods for moderate to long periods to bridge production and consumption cycles.

pairs.match: Receiving daily shipments from 200 suppliers, sorting cartons on high-speed conveyors, and loading outbound store trucks the same evening.
pairs.explanation: Distribution centers are designed to move goods rapidly through the channel rather than store them long term.

pairs.match: Delivering car seats to an assembly line only hours before installation so the factory holds minimal buffer stock.
pairs.explanation: JIT systems minimize inventory carrying and obsolescence costs by timing deliveries precisely to production need.

pairs.match: Shipping sealed containers by ocean vessel to a port, transferring them onto rail flatcars for the cross-country leg, and finishing delivery by truck.
pairs.explanation: Intermodal transportation combines two or more transport modes to balance cost, speed, and door-to-door reach.

question_text: A consumer instructs an autonomous AI shopping agent to find and buy a 27-inch 4K monitor under 350 dollars with at least a three-year warranty. Which set of classic channel functions does the AI agent perform directly, and which set must still be handled by underlying fulfillment networks?
hint: Distinguish transaction-completing software tasks from physical possession and logistics.
correct_answer_citation: Week 9: The AI Shopping Agent as a New Channel Intermediary

options.option_text: The AI agent performs physical distribution and warehousing directly, while retail storefronts perform matching and negotiation.
options.option_explanation: A software agent cannot physically store or transport a monitor. It performs the information and matching work instead.

options.option_text: The AI agent takes legal title and bears inventory obsolescence risk, while the manufacturer handles consumer search.
options.option_explanation: The AI shopping agent does not take physical possession or title to merchandise.

options.option_text: The AI agent performs information, contact, matching, and checkout execution directly, while physical distribution, warehousing, and reverse logistics remain with fulfillment networks.
options.option_explanation: Correct. The AI agent acts as a digital intermediary for the transaction-completing functions, while physical fulfillment still moves through warehouses and carriers.

options.option_text: The AI agent eliminates all eight channel functions so that neither software intermediaries nor logistics networks are needed.
options.option_explanation: Eliminating or replacing a traditional intermediary never eliminates the underlying channel functions that must be performed.
